notes: No source gives a ramp-up period for the programme mix. The state's own ag report assumes a 10-year rollout for irrigation-system upgrades, while leasing is described as near-term (could be at full scale within 1-2 seasons). 3 years is a reasonable blended central value, but the high end should extend to 10 years to cover infrastructure-heavy programmes.

quote: Municipal and industrial depletions have not changed substantially since 1989. After peaking at 385 KAF in 2020, depletions declined ... to 325 KAF in 2023.
source_title: Great Salt Lake 2025: Data and Insights

extra_sources.title: Great Salt Lake Data and Insights Summary
extra_sources.quote: Since 2015, residential depletions grew by 26.7%, while the population increased by 16.3%.

extra_sources.title: M&I Water Conservation Opportunities handout
extra_sources.quote: M&I diversion will increase but depletion needs to stay the same (or less).

arithmetic: 92 / 325 KAF (2023 M&I depletion) = 28% growth; this would match roughly a 28% basin population increase 2025-2055 at constant per-capita depletion, but no source states it.
notes: Searched strike_2025, strike_2026, gardner_proj, dwr_gsl, DWR regional M&I goals (2019) and the 2025 DWR M&I Conservation Opportunities report for a projected 2055 M&I depletion increase; none states 92 KAF/yr or a comparable figure. Evidence is mixed: M&I depletion was flat 1989-2023 while population doubled (implies a low draw), but residential depletion has grown faster than population since 2015 (implies a high draw). Keep the 40-180 range; relabel as derived/assumption unless a projection is found (the Gardner Utah 2065 basin-population projection plus 2024 per-capita residential depletion would be the way to derive it).

extra_sources.quote: about 25% of secondary connections in the state were metered in 2019-2020, increasing to about 35% metered in 2023. When the metered usage is normalized by the number of connections, the average metered usage per connection has not shifted meaningfully

notes: Searched Strike Team 2025/2026, the DWRi DMP page, the 2026 ag report, the 2025 DWR M&I report (Appendix K on metering) and web literature on metering effects on agricultural diversions. Sources say measurement is necessary for shepherding but give no delivery-share gain. The metering literature measures demand reduction (e.g. ~20% in older Utah planning only when paired with pricing; no clear effect from metering alone in the SEKID, BC study), not the share of saved water that reaches the lake. The 10-point cap remains a judgement.

These values reflect only cloud seeding efforts conducted within the Great Salt Lake Basin to date, although there is potential to increase the cloud seeding application area.

extra_sources.title: Utah Cloud Seeding Program: Increased Runoff and Cost Analyses
extra_sources.quote: The sum of estimated average annual increase in runoff for all of the projects is 186,663 acre-feet ... The increase in runoff for the Northern Utah Project is 50,698 acre-feet.

extra_sources.title: Great Salt Lake FAQ
extra_sources.quote: Historic cloud seeding evaluations have shown increases in the 6-12% range. However, Utah has modernized and expanded its program ... The goal is to increase precipitation by 15-20%.

arithmetic: DWR 2018 Table 4 GSL-basin target areas: Cache 37,341 + West Box Elder 13,357 + Tooele 4,160 + Western Uintas 22,364 = 77,222 AF/yr of existing added runoff. DWR 2025 gives 102,000 (Table H-4 labels it ac-ft/year; the text says 2017-2022, which is ambiguous, and as a 6-year total it would be ~17 KAF/yr).
notes: Existing seeding in the GSL basin is already credited with roughly 50-100 KAF/yr of added runoff. If cloud_cap means added runoff from new or expanded seeding, then 50 is plausible: the programme's stated goal is a 15-20% increase versus a historical 6-12%. If it means the whole programme, then 77-102 is the official estimate. Keep the 20-100 range. The DWR estimates are explicitly uncertain.

extra_sources.title: Price elasticity reconsidered: Panel estimation of an agricultural water demand function (Schoengold, Sunding, Moreno), WRR 42 W09411
extra_sources.quote: Estimation results indicate that the price elasticity of agricultural water demand is -0.79

notes: The model coefficient is not a price elasticity: it scales the charge relative to the net value of the water. The original Wiley PDF was blocked; the abstract was read via Crossref/EarthRef and the full working-paper version via AgEcon Search.

extra_sources.quote: Filling the lake in 30 years to the low end of the healthy range ... (4,198 feet) – will require between 471,000 and 1,055,000 acre-feet per year of additional water delivered to the lake.
extra_sources.locator: PDF p.4; Appendix Table 2, p.38 (471 = contemporary 1,643 kaf/yr inflow; 1,055 = drought 1,059 kaf/yr inflow)

extra_sources.title: Great Salt Lake 2025: Data and Insights
extra_sources.quote: Additional 770 KAF/year inflow scenario shows the expected inflow needed each year to reach a mean lake elevation of 4,198 feet by 2054.

arithmetic: Strike Team 2026: needed mean inflow ~2,465 KAF/yr minus the 2000-2025 average 1,665 KAF/yr = 800 KAF/yr. 1,665 equals the model's baseline_inflow, so 800 is the internally consistent target.
notes: The 471-1,055 range is confirmed verbatim in the Strategic Plan (Tarboton 2023 appendix). 875 appears in no source. The most recent official figure on the same 2000-2025 baseline that the model uses is 800 KAF/yr (March 2026), up from 770 in the January 2025 report. Keep the range at 471-1,055.

extra_sources.title: M&I Water Conservation Opportunities handout
extra_sources.quote: Turf Replacement Programs ... Potential depletion savings: 183,000 – 219,000 ac-ft ... Potential water savings: 429,000 – 492,000 ac-ft

arithmetic: Upper bound from the DWR turf figures: depletion savings / water savings = 183/429 = 0.43 to 219/492 = 0.45. At most ~0.44 of water not applied is freed depletion, before any reuse by growth or downstream diverters.
notes: Neither dwr_gsl nor the DMP page states a share. Sources only say that conserved city water reaches the lake if it is dedicated by change application or effluent dedication. 0.25 is plausible: about 0.44 depletion fraction times roughly 0.5-0.6 not re-used. It should be relabelled as an assumption. A suggested range of 0.1-0.45 is bounded above by the depletion fraction.

source_title: Opportunities and Costs for Agricultural Water Optimization in the Great Salt Lake Basin

extra_sources.title: 2023 Irrigation and Water Management Survey
extra_sources.quote: Utah ... Alfalfa ... 523,658 [acres] 2.4 [average acre-feet applied per acre]

arithmetic: Per AF depleted: $355/acre / 1.50 AF/acre = $236/AF (as stated). Per AF applied: $355 / 2.4 AF/acre (NASS 2023 Utah) = $148/AF; $355 / 2.64 = $134/AF, which reproduces the model's 133, so 133 appears to be a per-AF-applied figure.
notes: The cited NASS Utah page does not publish a net value of water. In the code the charge applies to depletion (charge_base is depletion), so the comparable figure is the forgone net return per AF depleted: $236/AF from the state's 2026 WTA analysis. The 133 value matches per AF applied only. Range: $148 (per AF applied) to $340-345 (costlier lease scenarios). Related: Table B-9 gives alfalfa expected returns of $304-361/acre, versus the model's hay_net_return of 175 $/acre (not in this batch).
